title: Dryer Not Heating? Diagnose Before Replacing the Heating Element
excerpt: No heat and slow drying are different problems. Learn which checks you can make, why thermal fuses need model-specific testing, and when to book dryer repair.
author: Elmir R.
content:
A dryer that tumbles without heat does not automatically need a heating element. Power supply, cycle settings, thermal protection, controls, and the heating system can all be involved. A dryer that gets warm but takes too long to dry may instead have an airflow or load problem. Describing that difference is more useful than ordering the cheapest part first.

Start with the symptom and model number

Note whether the drum turns, whether it ever warms up, whether it stops early, and whether an error or check-vent message appears. Find the model number on the appliance label and use the troubleshooting section of that model's manual. Gas, conventional electric, and heat-pump dryers do not use the same heating system.

An electric dryer's motor can run even when the supply needed for heating is incomplete. That is one reason a turning drum does not rule out an electrical supply problem. Do not open an outlet or test live wiring yourself; have a qualified professional check the supply if needed.

Checks you can make without opening the dryer

  • Check that a heated cycle is selected rather than an air-only setting.
  • Clean the lint screen according to the manual and avoid overloading the drum.
  • Notice whether clothes leave the washer unusually wet. A washer spin problem can look like a dryer problem.
  • Look for a visibly crushed exhaust duct without moving or disconnecting the appliance.
  • If the outside vent is safely accessible, check for a visible obstruction. Leave elevated outlets and inaccessible ductwork to a professional.

Vented dryers need a clear exhaust route to the outdoors. Ventless dryers have different maintenance requirements, such as filters or a condenser, described in their own manuals. Do not apply vented-dryer instructions to a heat-pump or condenser model.

What a thermal fuse does, and what it does not prove

A thermal fuse is a one-time safety device. Depending on the dryer design, an open fuse or thermal cutoff may interrupt heat or prevent operation altogether. It is not a resettable switch, and its effect cannot be assumed from the brand name alone.

A technician uses the model's wiring information and appropriate tests to check the relevant thermal devices, heating or ignition circuit, and controls. A failed fuse also calls for a check of the conditions that caused overheating. Replacing a fuse without addressing the cause can leave the underlying fault unresolved.

There is no universal replacement fuse for every Whirlpool, Kenmore, or Maytag dryer. Order parts by the complete model number and manufacturer compatibility information. Never bypass a fuse, substitute a different rating, or operate with panels removed.

Keep the exhaust connected during operation

Never test a vented dryer by running it with the exhaust disconnected indoors. Gas dryer exhaust can contain combustion products, and any vented dryer releases heat, lint, and moisture through its exhaust. Ask for an airflow and vent inspection using the manufacturer's procedure instead.

Stop using a dryer that overheats or smells burnt. If you smell gas, leave the building immediately without operating switches, appliances, or a phone inside. From a safe location outdoors, call 911 or your gas utility. Arrange appliance repair after the emergency has been addressed.

What to ask before approving a repair

Ask which component failed testing, whether the exhaust or supply also needs attention, and whether the correct replacement part is available. A small part price by itself is not the installed repair price; diagnosis, access, labor, and the specific model all affect the quote.

For dryer repair in our Connecticut service area, My Appliance Repair charges a $99 service call for diagnosis, waived when you proceed with repair. Your technician provides a written repair quote on-site before work begins. Request a repair visit and include the model number, fuel type, and symptoms. Our team confirms coverage and appointment availability.

Manufacturer references

  • Whirlpool: dryer not heating troubleshooting
  • Whirlpool: checking dryer venting
  • Whirlpool owner manual: outdoor exhaust requirements for a vented dryer
seoTitle: Dryer Not Heating? Check This Before the Heating Element

title: Newer isn't always better for washing machines
excerpt: Washing machine repair in Connecticut doesn't always mean replacing it. Why older top-loaders outlast newer HE machines — and when the math actually works.
author: Elmir R.
content:
I had a woman call me from Glastonbury last spring about her Samsung front-loader throwing an ND error code. Four years old, not draining. The culprit was a seized drain pump — part DC31-00054A, about $35 for the part. Straightforward washing machine repair. But while I was there she mentioned her mother's 2004 Maytag top-loader was sitting in the basement and she was about to donate it. I plugged it in and ran it through a cycle. Thing worked perfectly. I told her that Maytag would probably outlast the Samsung by a solid decade. She wasn't thrilled to hear it. She kept the Maytag.

That visit stuck with me because it's a pattern I keep seeing across Connecticut. The newer machine struggling at year four. The older machine still running at year nineteen. And the customer surprised, because everything they've read tells them newer is better.

What actually breaks — and what it costs

The type of failure tells you almost everything about whether a washing machine repair is worth doing. Older mechanical machines fail mechanically. Newer machines fail electronically. Those two failure types have completely different cost profiles.

Common failures on pre-2012 top-loaders:

  • Lid switch (WP3949247) — about $14, 25 minutes to replace. Machine fills and agitates but won't spin. This is the single most common failure on late-2000s Whirlpool top-loaders.
  • Drive belt — $10 to $20, straightforward swap.
  • Pump impeller — usually something caught in it. $15 to $35 for the part.
  • Inlet valve — $20 to $40, fixes slow-fill or no-fill issues.

These parts have been made by aftermarket suppliers for years and will keep being made because the underlying designs haven't changed. The total repair price depends on the diagnosis, part availability, and labor. A technician can compare an on-site repair quote with the cost of replacing the washer.

Common failures on newer HE front-loaders:

  • Control board failure on a Samsung WF45R6100AW — replacement board alone runs $180 to $240, before a technician even arrives. That machine retailed around $699. You're already at or past the 50% rule on parts alone, on a machine that might be five years old.
  • Door boot seal — see the section below. Not as expensive, but a recurring cost a top-loader never has.
  • Drum bearings — labor-intensive to access on front-loaders. By the time you pay for that work, you're most of the way to a replacement anyway.

That's the core problem with newer high-efficiency washers. When the board goes, the washing machine repair math usually doesn't work. Most of the time I tell people straight: don't fix it.

Is it worth repairing your washing machine? The efficiency argument has a hole in it

Yes, a modern HE washer uses less water per cycle — somewhere around 13 to 15 gallons compared to 30 to 40 gallons for an older top-loader with a full agitator. That's a real difference. But if you're doing six loads a week in a Connecticut household, you're saving maybe $30 to $50 a year on water depending on your municipal rate.

A control-board repair can offset years of water savings, so compare the actual repair quote with the savings you expect. The efficiency math only works if the machine stays healthy, and a lot of them don't. So when customers ask whether repairing a washing machine is worth it, the answer almost always comes down to machine age and failure type — not how efficient it is on the spec sheet.

Door boot seals and the mold problem

Front-loaders trap moisture in the rubber gasket around the door. On Samsung and LG front-loaders from roughly 2017 to 2021, I've seen a consistent pattern of door boot seal failures showing up around year four or five. The seal — DC64-00802C on several Samsung models — develops micro-tears, harbors mold, and eventually starts letting water past.

Hard water accelerates this. If you're on a well in northern Connecticut, you'll likely see it sooner. The replacement itself isn't terrible — about 45 minutes of work. But it's a cost that a top-loader with a simple hinged lid simply never has.

Parts availability is a real thing nobody mentions at the store

Manufacturers aren't required to stock parts indefinitely. Some brands stop producing electronic components for a specific model within seven years of its last production run. I've had Connecticut customers with machines from 2019 where I couldn't source a control board through any normal channel by 2025.

Meanwhile I can get mechanical components for a 2001 Whirlpool direct-drive transmission from three different aftermarket suppliers by tomorrow morning. That gap doesn't show up in any spec sheet — but it will show up the day you need a washing machine repair and the part simply doesn't exist anymore.

When to fix an older machine — and when to walk away

Fix it if:

  • It's a mechanical failure on a pre-2012 top-loader (lid switch, pump, belt, inlet valve)
  • The on-site repair quote is reasonable compared with the cost of a comparable replacement
  • The machine was originally built to run 15-plus years and has no bearing noise

Walk away if:

  • It's a control board failure on any machine that retailed under $600 — the numbers rarely work regardless of age
  • It's a front-loader with bearing noise at year six or seven — start shopping
  • The repair estimate exceeds 50% of the machine's current replacement cost

Honestly, a used 2005 to 2008 Whirlpool or Maytag top-loader in decent shape can be a smarter buy than a new budget front-loader. When I evaluate one, I listen for grinding on the bearing during spin, check that the agitator dogs are grabbing properly, run the lid switch test, and smell for any burning on the motor during spin. Those four things tell you what you're actually buying.

Washing machine repair in our Connecticut service communities

My Appliance Repair serves customers in our listed Connecticut service communities. If your washer is acting up, the fastest way to get clarity is to contact our team and describe the symptom before you do anything else. Sometimes it's a $14 part. Sometimes it's a conversation about replacement. We'll tell you which one honestly, because that's what we'd want someone to tell us.

Don't let a four-year-old machine with a control-board problem make you feel like washing machine repair is always a bad bet. The math on older mechanical machines is completely different from the math on newer electronic ones. If you're not sure which situation you're in, go ahead and book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll figure out what you're actually dealing with. If the diagnosis points to a repair that makes sense, we'll do it. If it doesn't, we'll tell you that too.

title: Refrigerator coils you never clean are costing you real money
excerpt: Dirty refrigerator condenser coils cost Connecticut homeowners up to $14/month in wasted electricity — and can kill a compressor early. Clean them in 15 minutes.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Last winter we got a call from a homeowner in Milford who was convinced her five-year-old LG French door fridge was dying. The compressor was running nonstop and the cabinet couldn't get below 40°F. She'd already been quoted a compressor replacement by another company. Before our technician even opened his bag, he popped the front grille off. The refrigerator condenser coils were so packed with dog hair from her two golden retrievers that he could barely see the fins underneath. Eight minutes with a brush. Two hours later the fridge was sitting at 37°F. The compressor quote she'd been given was $480 — just for the part.

That's not a fluke. Here at My Appliance Repair, we see a version of that call more than we'd like to.

Where the condenser coils actually are on your fridge

On most modern bottom-freezer and French door units, the refrigerator condenser coils sit behind a grille at the front bottom of the machine. That grille snaps off with no tools — homeowners are genuinely surprised every time we show them. Older top-freezer models — Whirlpool and Maytag from the mid-2010s especially — sometimes have rear-mounted coils on the back of the unit. Those collect a little less debris but still deserve a look every couple of years.

Built-ins and some counter-depth models are a different story. Those can have coils tucked behind a rear access panel that requires partial disassembly to reach. Not a 15-minute job on those. If you're in Connecticut and you're not sure what you're getting into, contact our team before you pull anything apart.

What clogged condenser coils do to a compressor

The condenser coils exist to shed heat. When they're matted with dust and pet hair, the compressor can't release heat efficiently — so it runs longer and hotter each cycle trying to maintain target temperature. Over months, that adds up to roughly $8–14 per month in wasted electricity on a full-size side-by-side, depending on your Connecticut utility rate. Over years, it shortens the compressor's life.

A compressor replacement requires an on-site diagnosis and written repair quote. Compare that quote with the cost of a comparable replacement, the appliance’s age, and any remaining warranty. Dirty refrigerator condenser coils are a contributing factor in roughly 20–30% of the premature compressor failures we diagnose — not the only cause, but a real and preventable one.

The sequence most people miss: skipped maintenance → compressor stress → a repair bill that exceeds the machine's value.

The pet hair problem is worse than you think

Homes with dogs and cats are the worst offenders by a wide margin. We've pulled coil mats off LG French door units that looked like something had nested there. The LG LRMVS3006 series and similar models have bottom-front coil placement with a grille that sits about two inches off the floor — in a house with a shedding dog, those refrigerator condenser coils fill up fast. It's worse if the fridge sits on carpet or near a return air vent.

If you have pets and you've never popped that grille off, the first cleaning is going to be the most important one you ever do.

How to clean refrigerator condenser coils in 15 minutes

What you need

  • A condenser coil cleaning brush (the Frigidaire 5303281153 is common — any generic equivalent works fine)
  • A vacuum with a soft brush attachment
  • About 15 minutes

Step-by-step

  1. Unplug the refrigerator before you start. Always disconnect power before working under or behind the unit.
  2. Snap off the front grille at the base of the fridge — no tools needed on most models.
  3. Work the coil brush carefully along the fins without bending them.
  4. Vacuum up what comes loose.
  5. Snap the grille back on, then plug the fridge back in.

The brush costs about $7–9 at any hardware store and lasts for years. Clean the coils once a year as a baseline — every six months if you have pets or the fridge lives in a dusty basement. If the fridge is six or more years old and you've never done this, do it this week.

Connecticut summers make this worse

Ambient kitchen temperatures climb in July and August, and the compressor already works harder to hold 37°F against the heat. Dirty refrigerator condenser coils compound that load directly. Connecticut homeowners feel this most during summer heat waves — it's a year-round maintenance issue, but if you've been putting it off, the warmest months are the costliest time to stay behind on it.

This is one of the few things you can do yourself that has a direct, measurable effect on how long a fridge lasts. Most maintenance advice is vague. This one isn't. Clean condenser coils → compressor runs less → compressor lasts longer. That's the whole chain.

When to call a technician instead

If your fridge is already running constantly, not holding temperature, or showing heavy frost buildup on the back wall of the freezer, dirty condenser coils may be part of the problem — but probably aren't the only thing going on. A clogged coil is a maintenance issue. A fridge that's already symptomatic is a diagnostic call.

Sometimes the damage is already done and the compressor is failing regardless. If cleaning the coils doesn't bring the machine back to normal within a few hours, that's when you want a technician to look at it properly. You can review our appliance repair services to get a sense of what that involves.

If you're already past the maintenance stage and something isn't right, book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll come take a look.
seoTitle: Dirty Refrigerator Coils Are Costing You Real Money

title: Cleaning the lint trap isn't enough
excerpt: Dryer lint trap cleaning every load isn't enough. Hidden lint in the blower wheel and trap slot slows dryers — and starts house fires. Connecticut dryer repair.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Dryer lint trap cleaning is a habit most Connecticut homeowners have down cold — pull the screen, peel off the lint, push it back in. But the lint screen catches maybe 70% of what your dryer produces. The fine particulate that slips through keeps moving: coating the inside of the trap slot, sticking to duct walls inside the cabinet, and packing itself into the blower wheel. After three to five years of regular use, that buildup is substantial — and nobody cleaned it because nobody knew to look there.

According to the U.S. Fire Administration, clothes dryers cause roughly 2,900 home fires every year. Most people point to the vent duct, but a significant share trace back to internal lint restriction that basic screen cleaning never reaches.

The screen is only the first filter in a longer path. What it misses creates the real problem — one we diagnose on dryer calls across Connecticut every week.

Why dryer lint trap cleaning is only half the job

Most homeowners treat dryer lint trap cleaning as a single step: remove the screen, peel off the visible layer, replace it. That habit is worth keeping. But the trap slot the screen lives in — and the blower wheel the airstream feeds into — collect lint the whole time, invisibly. Those two areas are where the real restriction builds, and neither one cleans itself.

Pull your lint screen out right now and look at the slot it lives in. Run your finger along the side walls. There's a felt-like gray layer built up in there, narrowing the airflow opening whether or not your screen is spotless. A narrow, flexible dryer lint brush costs about $8 at any hardware store. That slot should get brushed out every three to six months. Most people do it never.

Where lint actually goes after the screen

Airflow in a dryer runs drum → lint screen → blower wheel → exhaust duct. Anything small enough to get past the screen rides the airstream straight into the blower housing. The blower wheel — the fan that pulls air through the machine — has fins designed to move air. Those same fins are perfect for catching fine lint. Over time they cake up, the wheel moves less air, and the dryer runs hotter and slower trying to compensate.

The trap slot compounds the problem. Even with consistent screen cleaning, the slot walls narrow over time. Brushing them out takes five minutes and costs nothing beyond the brush. It's the single most overlooked maintenance step on any dryer.

The blower wheel: what restricted airflow actually looks like

We pulled a Whirlpool dryer for a customer in Milford last year. She'd had her exhaust vent professionally cleaned six months before, so she ruled that out and figured the heating element was failing. We removed the back panel, ran the machine for two minutes, and watched the blower wheel barely turn — it was so packed with lint it had almost no clearance. Heat was building inside the cabinet because air had nowhere to go fast enough.

We cleared the wheel, brushed out the slot, and put the panel back on. She ran a full load of towels in 47 minutes. Parts: nothing. Her dryer had been limping along for almost a year — running two full cycles per load — because of internal lint buildup she didn't know to address.

Whirlpool and Maytag dryers from roughly 2015 to 2022 are the machines we open most often with this problem. The exhaust path routing on those models pulls lint past the screen faster than some other designs. Samsung gas dryers from the same era show it too, sometimes faster. If we run ten dryer calls in a week across Connecticut, two or three trace back to internal lint restriction — not a failed component.

The thermal fuse that keeps blowing

On Whirlpool machines, the thermal fuse is part number 3392519 — about $6. It's a one-time safety device that cuts power to the heating circuit when the dryer overheats. When airflow is restricted by a packed blower wheel, temperatures inside the cabinet climb, and the fuse blows to protect the machine. That's the fuse doing exactly what it's supposed to do.

But here's the pattern we see constantly: customer replaces the fuse, dryer works, fuse blows again four to six months later. They replace it again. Now they think the dryer is dying. It's not. The fuse is a symptom. The restricted airflow is the cause. Until you fix the airflow — which means going beyond dryer lint trap cleaning to the blower wheel itself — you'll keep buying fuses.

What you can do yourself — and what you probably can't

DIY: cleaning the lint trap slot

The lint slot is a genuine DIY job. Here's how to do it:

  • Pull the lint screen completely out of the slot
  • Insert a flexible dryer lint brush into the slot and work it down both sides
  • Pull out whatever the brush brings up — the first pass after a few years will surprise you
  • Repeat every three to six months to keep it manageable

This takes about five minutes and costs nothing beyond the brush. It's something every Connecticut homeowner can do without touching a panel or a wire.

Professional: cleaning the blower wheel

The blower wheel is a different story. Getting to it usually means removing the front or rear panel depending on the brand, disconnecting a few wires, and knowing what you're looking at once you're inside. If you're comfortable with basic appliance disassembly, it's manageable. If you're not, don't guess. A clogged blower on a machine that's otherwise fine is a $45–$85 parts job if the wheel needs replacing, plus labor — and it's worth doing right.

At My Appliance Repair, we handle this regularly for homeowners across Connecticut who assumed their dryer needed a new part when all it needed was a thorough cleaning. You can book a service call and we'll tell you honestly what we find.

Don't replace the heating element until you've checked airflow

A heating element on a standard electric dryer runs $30–$55 in parts, and it's a reasonable fix when the element has actually failed. But a clogged blower wheel mimics a bad element symptom for symptom:

  • Long drying times even on high heat
  • Clothes still damp at the end of a full cycle
  • Heat that feels weaker than it used to
  • Dryer running multiple cycles to finish one load

We've seen Connecticut customers spend money on a new heating element and have the exact same problem a month later because nobody checked the blower. The part didn't fix it — the airflow did. In most of those cases, cleaning the internal components was the only repair needed.

If your dryer has been running slow for more than a few months and a vent cleaning didn't solve it, contact our team or have someone pull the panel and check the blower before you buy anything. It's usually faster to diagnose than people expect.

Connecticut dryer repair: what we see in the field

We service dryers across Connecticut — from Fairfield County through Hartford and into the shoreline towns. Call volume on slow, overheating dryers spikes every fall when households start running heavier loads. The overwhelming majority of those calls are not mechanical failures. They're maintenance problems: lint where it shouldn't be, airflow that's half what it should be, and a machine that was never told to do anything except run.

Towns like Milford, Shelton, Derby, and Ansonia send us a steady stream of Whirlpool and Samsung dryers with exactly the blower restriction described above. New Haven and Hamden calls trend toward older Maytag units where the slot hasn't been brushed in five or more years. The geography changes the brand mix slightly — the root cause almost never changes.

If you're in Connecticut and want My Appliance Repair to take a look, schedule a repair and we'll sort out what's actually going on.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I clean more than just the lint screen?

Brush out the lint trap slot every three to six months. The blower wheel should be inspected every two to three years, or sooner if drying times are increasing or the machine is running unusually hot.

Can a dirty blower wheel start a fire?

Yes. Lint packed around the blower wheel restricts airflow, which causes heat to build inside the cabinet. That's one of the primary internal ignition sources the U.S. Fire Administration tracks — separate from vent duct fires that most people think of first.

My dryer vent was just cleaned. Why is it still slow?

Vent cleaning addresses the exhaust duct from the cabinet to the outside wall. It does nothing to the internal blower wheel or lint trap slot. If the vent is clear and the dryer is still slow, the restriction is almost certainly inside the machine — and that's where we look first.

Is dryer lint trap cleaning enough if I do it every load?

Cleaning the screen every load is the right habit, but it only captures lint large enough to be caught by the mesh. Finer particles pass through and accumulate in the slot and blower housing over time. Screen cleaning alone will not prevent internal buildup.

title: Ice maker died again? It's probably not the ice maker.
excerpt: Ice maker not making ice? In most Connecticut homes, the culprit is a clogged water valve or old filter — not the ice maker. Here's what to check first.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Last spring I got a call from a guy in Branford who had already ordered a $200 ice maker assembly off Amazon. It was sitting on his counter in the box when I got there. The water inlet valve was clogged. He sent the assembly back unopened.

This is the most common version of the ice-maker-not-making-ice story. The ice maker gets blamed because it's the visible thing, the thing with a name, the thing that stopped doing its job. But on most service calls here in Connecticut, the ice maker is the victim, not the cause. Before you order anything or call anyone, run through the checklist below.

Why your ice maker is not making ice: quick checklist

These are the seven most common reasons an ice maker stops making ice — roughly in order of how often we see them on service calls across Connecticut.

Most likely causes

  • Water inlet valve clogged or failing
  • Water filter overdue for replacement
  • Freezer temperature running too warm
  • Kinked or frozen water supply line
  • Low household water pressure
  • Bail arm stuck in the off position
  • Ice maker module or mold thermostat failure

Most of these take ten minutes to check yourself. Here's what to look for on each one.

The water inlet valve: the first place to look

The water inlet valve is a small electrically controlled valve that opens to let water into the ice maker. They wear out, they clog with mineral deposits, and when they fail the ice maker either cycles through its routine and produces nothing, or makes those thin hollow cubes that fall apart when you touch them. Valve replacement runs $40 to $80 in parts depending on the brand — a long way from a full ice maker assembly.

Classic symptom: Ice maker not making ice, but you can hear it cycling — nothing comes out. That's almost always the inlet valve, not the module.

A lot of the time the module is fine and the valve isn't opening fully. This is the first thing we check on a service call, and it's the first thing you should check at home.

The water filter nobody's touched in three years

Before you call anyone, go find your water filter. If you can't remember when you changed it last, change it now. A clogged filter creates enough flow restriction to starve the ice maker, and the result looks exactly like a hardware failure: no drama, no error code, just no ice.

About half the people I talk to don't know where their filter is, or didn't know the fridge had one. Some in-door filter housings hide them pretty well. A few things worth knowing:

  • Most manufacturers recommend replacement every six months
  • Once a year is realistic for most Connecticut households
  • Three years is not fine — and it's one of the most common reasons we find for ice maker not making ice on service calls

Freezer temperature and water pressure

Ice makers have a built-in cutoff. If the freezer runs above roughly 10°F, the ice maker shuts itself off. That's actually it working correctly — protecting itself from making a mess. So if your freezer is running warm because the evaporator fan is struggling or the door gasket has been leaking cold air for the last eight months, the ice maker isn't broken. It's just waiting for conditions that aren't coming.

Check your freezer temp with a cheap thermometer before assuming anything. If it's reading 18 or 20 degrees, a warm freezer — not a broken ice maker — is why you're not getting ice.

Water pressure is worth checking at the same time. Manufacturers typically require at least 20 PSI at the valve. A quick way to test it: dispense water into a measuring cup for ten seconds — you should get at least six ounces. If you come up short, remove the water filter and try again. A clogged filter is often the culprit, but if pressure is still low without it, the issue may be further upstream.

Check the water line behind the fridge

This one takes ten minutes. Pull the fridge out and look at the water line. Kinked lines are more common than they should be, especially after someone slid the fridge back in a hurry. And in older Connecticut homes where kitchen plumbing runs near an exterior wall, that line can freeze in a bad winter. We've seen this in Waterbury and New Haven a handful of times, usually in January. It thaws out, works fine, nobody ever knew.

Samsung, Whirlpool, and LG ice makers: what's different

The checklist above applies to most refrigerator brands, but a few are worth calling out specifically:

  • Samsung: The French door models have a well-documented ice maker freezing problem — the ice maker itself freezes over and stops cycling. This is a design issue, not user error, and it requires defrosting the unit and in some cases a duct cover fix.
  • Whirlpool / Maytag: The modular ice maker design on many side-by-side models has a common mold thermostat failure point. Worth testing before replacing the full assembly.
  • LG: Certain LG models with the craft ice feature have had known issues with the lower ice maker. If your LG is producing no ice at all, check for a software or sensor issue before assuming mechanical failure.

If you're not sure what you're dealing with, brand-specific diagnosis is part of what My Appliance Repair does on every service call across Connecticut.

When the ice maker itself is actually the problem

It does happen. The bail arm gets stuck in the off position, the mold thermostat fails, the motor burns out. If you need the full assembly replaced on a Samsung or Whirlpool, you're looking at $150 to $250 in parts plus labor. That's a reasonable fix on a fridge that's under eight or ten years old. On a fifteen-year-old unit, the conversation gets more complicated — and at My Appliance Repair, we'll tell you that honestly before you spend anything.

You can take a look at our appliance repair services to get a sense of what we cover. If you want a straight answer about whether something's worth fixing, just contact our team and we'll give you an honest assessment before any money changes hands.

But do the easy stuff first. Filter, temperature, water pressure, water line. Half the time you've already solved the ice-maker-not-making-ice problem before anyone shows up. If you haven't, book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll start with the valve — not the part you already ordered off Amazon.

Common questions about ice makers not making ice

How long does it take for an ice maker to start working again after I fix the issue?

Most ice makers need 24 hours to resume normal production after a repair or filter change. If yours still isn't producing ice after a full day, there may be a secondary issue worth investigating.

Can a bad water filter really stop ice production completely?

Yes. A severely clogged filter can reduce water flow enough that the ice maker receives no water at all — making it look like a complete hardware failure. It's the easiest thing to rule out and should always be the first step.

Is it worth repairing an ice maker on an older refrigerator?

Generally yes, if the fridge is under ten years old and the repair is limited to the valve or filter. On older units or when the compressor is also showing signs of trouble, it's worth having an honest conversation about cost versus replacement — which is exactly what we do on every Connecticut service call.

title: Leaving food in your fridge when the power goes out costs you more than you think
excerpt: Power outage refrigerator food safety starts with one rule: keep the door closed. What to save, what to toss, and how to protect your fridge — from a Connecticut repair team.
author: Elmir R.
content:
A woman in Meriden called us after a storm last spring. Power had been out for about eight hours, and she'd opened the fridge maybe five or six times to check on things. "Just a quick look," she kept saying. She lost everything — and with basic power outage refrigerator food safety knowledge, most of it could have been saved.

That call happens more than you'd think. So here's what the team at My Appliance Repair tells people standing in their kitchen the day after a Connecticut storm — because it saves food, and sometimes it saves your compressor too.

How long your refrigerator actually stays safe during a power outage

The four-hour window

A closed refrigerator holds a safe temperature for roughly four hours during a power outage. A packed freezer can hold it for a full day or two. The word that matters in both of those sentences is closed.

Every time you open the door you're letting cold air fall out and warm air pour in. It's not dramatic — it just adds up fast. Five "quick looks" over eight hours and you've blown the whole window. The fridge can't tell you whether your leftovers are okay by you staring at them. A thermometer can. Most people don't own one. A basic refrigerator thermometer runs about six dollars and is worth having before you need it.

If the outage is going to run long

If it looks like power won't be back within a few hours, move what matters most into a cooler with ice before the four-hour mark — don't wait until after. Prioritize:

  • Deli meat and opened packages of poultry or fish
  • Opened dairy — milk, cream, soft cheeses
  • Anything already cooked
  • Items with eggs or mayo

Leave condiments where they are. More on that below.

Power outage refrigerator food safety: what to throw out and what to keep

The core rule for power outage refrigerator food safety is 40°F. If your fridge has been above that temperature for more than two hours, certain things have to go. No exceptions:

  • Cooked meat, poultry, and fish
  • Cut fruit and leafy greens
  • Soft cheeses and opened dairy
  • Anything with eggs in it — casseroles, quiche, custards
  • Opened mayo and creamy dressings
  • Leftover takeout

Condiments are more forgiving than people think. Ketchup, mustard, pickles, hard cheeses, butter, and whole fruits and vegetables are not the things that get you sick. It's cooked proteins and dairy-heavy items you need to be honest about.

If you don't have a thermometer and you're guessing — that's exactly what it is. A guess. Food poisoning from spoiled chicken is not a fun way to spend a Tuesday.

Freezer food safety: the rules after a power outage

Everyone asks the same thing: "Is it still frozen?" And they want the answer to be yes. The real question is whether it partially thawed and refroze, because that's what actually causes problems.

  • Safe: Meat that's still cold and firm all the way to the center.
  • Discard: Anything soft in the middle, or with visible pooled liquid in the bag — that refroze.

Ice crystals on the surface don't tell you much. "Still has some ice on it" is not the same as "safe to eat." The freezer is more forgiving than the fridge during a power outage, but it has limits too. A full freezer holds temperature significantly longer than a half-empty one — another reason to keep it stocked during Connecticut storm season.

The fridge damage that shows up two days later

This is the part no food safety guide covers, because they're not written by appliance technicians. Power coming back isn't always gentle. Voltage spikes on restore hit your refrigerator's electrical components hard — especially the start relay and the control board.

We got a call in Waterbury last winter, two days after a big storm. Three-year-old Samsung, completely dead. Compressor not running, not cold. The customer had a surge protector on his TV, his router, his gaming setup — nothing on the fridge. The control board was fried. That was a $280 repair. A decent surge protector for an appliance outlet runs about $25.

Parts most likely to fail after a power outage

  • Start relay: $40–$80 for the part. One of the most common failures we see after outage events.
  • Control board: $200 or more on newer Samsung and LG units with advanced electronics.
  • Compressor: Less common, but voltage irregularities on restore can stress it over time.

If your refrigerator is plugged into a plain wall outlet with no surge protection right now, that's the single easiest thing you can change before the next storm hits Connecticut.

What to do after the power comes back on

Give the compressor time to stabilize

Wait 15 to 20 minutes before loading food back into the refrigerator. Let the compressor cycle up and stabilize. Listen for it — a healthy compressor starts up, runs for a bit, then goes quiet. It should do that several times in the first hour.

Signs something is wrong

If the compressor is running constantly and the temperature isn't dropping, that's a problem. Either the compressor is struggling or something in the sealed system took damage. Watch the temp over the next two to three hours. If it's not back down to the mid-30s by then, stop loading food into it and call someone.

At My Appliance Repair, we're happy to help you figure out what you're dealing with before you commit to a service visit. Contact our team and describe what you're hearing — we can usually tell you over the phone whether it warrants a visit or whether the unit just needs more time to recover. We'd rather spend two minutes on a call than have you throw out another fridge full of food unnecessarily.

Before the next Connecticut storm: your power outage refrigerator food safety checklist

Connecticut storm season runs from spring thunderstorms straight through to nor'easters in late fall. Good power outage refrigerator food safety habits start before the outage — not during it. Here's the short list:

  • Put a $6 refrigerator thermometer inside your fridge today
  • Plug your refrigerator into a surge-protected outlet
  • Keep a cooler and ice packs on hand during storm season
  • Resist the urge to open the door during an outage
  • Know your four-hour window — and act before it closes

If you want to know more about what we handle, take a look at our appliance repair services.

If your refrigerator is acting up after a recent power outage — not cooling, running constantly, or completely dead — don't wait to see if it works itself out. Book a service call with My Appliance Repair and we'll come take a look. Better to catch a start relay early than replace a control board later.

title: Refrigerators die younger than they used to, and here's why
excerpt: Modern refrigerators fail years sooner than older models. A Connecticut refrigerator repair technician explains the real reasons why — and how to protect yours.
author: Elmir R.
content:
The "they don't make 'em like they used to" thing is usually nostalgia talking. With refrigerators, it's actually true — and I say that as someone who does refrigerator repair in Connecticut for a living, not as someone who's bitter about progress.

Had a call in Naugatuck about six weeks ago. Samsung side-by-side, seven years old, second compressor failure. The couple who owned it kept asking what they were doing wrong. Nothing. They were doing nothing wrong. The machine just isn't built with the same margin for error that older units were.

What actually changed in modern refrigerator design

Modern fridges run inverter compressors, which are more efficient but more sensitive — especially to voltage fluctuations and heat. Manufacturers also thinned out the insulation to hit energy efficiency ratings. Tighter tolerances, less buffer. And there are more electronics now: control boards, thermistors, door sensors, ice maker modules. Every one of those is a failure point that didn't exist on a 1994 Whirlpool top-freezer that's still running in someone's garage right now.

French door and bottom-freezer designs put the compressor down near the floor, where it's warmer and where dust and pet hair collect faster. That matters more than people think, and it's one of the first things we check on a refrigerator repair call here in Connecticut.

The brands we see most often on service calls

We're not here to trash anyone, but we'd be doing you a disservice if we didn't say this: Samsung sealed system failures and LG linear compressor failures are something the team at My Appliance Repair sees constantly across Connecticut. The LG linear compressor issue is well-documented in the trade. A lot of those units are dying at five or six years old. We've seen it enough times that when someone calls with a newer LG French door that stopped cooling, we already have a pretty good idea what we're walking into.

Older GE and Whirlpool top-freezers from the nineties? Still running. Newer versions of those same brands are a different story too, though not quite as bad in our experience.

Refrigerator maintenance Connecticut homeowners can actually control

Most refrigerator problems we see in Connecticut homes could have been delayed — or avoided — with a few simple habits. Here's what makes the biggest difference:

Simple steps that extend your fridge's life

  • Clean the condenser coils once a year. They're under the fridge or behind it, depending on the model. It takes ten minutes and a vacuum. Dust and pet hair make the compressor work harder and run hotter, shortening its life. This is the single most skipped maintenance item we see on refrigerator repair calls.
  • Check your door gasket. Close the door on a dollar bill and pull it out. You should feel resistance. If it slides right out, the gasket is soft and your compressor is running constantly trying to compensate.
  • Don't install it with zero clearance. Counter-depth and built-in setups look great, but if heat has nowhere to go, you're slowly cooking the compressor. The manual has clearance specs for a reason.
  • Don't wait if it's running warm. If it's running all the time and the inside is warm, call someone soon. The food loss will cost you more than the repair bill if you wait two weeks.

Should you repair or replace your refrigerator?

Here’s how we talk through it with customers: the technician diagnoses the fault on-site and provides a written quote. Compressor, sealed-system, and control-board work can require very different parts and labor. Compare the actual refrigerator repair quote with the cost of a comparable replacement, the age and condition of the fridge, and any warranty coverage. The $99 service call fee covers the diagnostic and is waived when you proceed with the repair.

Had a couple in Cheshire last spring with a six-year-old LG French door, linear compressor gone. They'd bought the extended warranty and it covered most of it. Honestly, extended warranties on refrigerators are one of the few times we think they actually make sense, given where the industry is right now. For most appliances we'd tell you to skip it. Fridges are the exception.

How do I know if my refrigerator compressor is failing?

The most common signs are: the fridge runs constantly but can't hold temperature, the motor feels hot to the touch at the back, or you hear a clicking or humming noise that starts and stops. Any of these on a newer unit warrants a call — catching a compressor issue early can mean the difference between a straightforward refrigerator repair and a full replacement.

Is it worth repairing a refrigerator that's less than 10 years old?

Usually, yes — with exceptions. If the repair is a sealed system or compressor replacement on a unit that's already had problems, the math can tip toward replacement. If it's a control board, door gasket, ice maker, or fan motor, repair almost always wins. Age alone isn't the deciding factor; the specific failure and the cost of a comparable replacement are.

When to call a Connecticut refrigerator repair technician

If your refrigerator is running constantly, not holding temperature, or making noises it didn't used to make, don't sit on it. The longer a compressor runs under stress, the more the repair costs — and at some point the repair window closes entirely. Connecticut homeowners who call early almost always spend less.

You can contact our team and describe what it's doing. Half the time the My Appliance Repair team can narrow it down before we even show up at your door. We serve homeowners in our listed Connecticut service communities, including Naugatuck and Cheshire.

None of this is doom and gloom. It's just: know what you bought, do the simple maintenance, and don't be surprised if a 2019 fridge needs work. It's not you.

If something's already wrong, go ahead and book a service call and we'll take a look. Sooner is usually cheaper.

title: What to Do When Your Appliances Lose Power: A Connecticut Storm Season Survival Guide
excerpt: Connecticut power outages damage appliances when electricity returns. Learn how to protect yours and when to call a Connecticut appliance repair pro.
author: My Appliance Repair Team
content:
Connecticut storms knock out power without warning—and the voltage surge when electricity returns is often what triggers an appliance repair call. If you've lived here for any length of time, you know the drill: dark clouds roll in, the wind picks up, and before long the lights are flickering. Whether it's a summer thunderstorm tearing through Fairfield County or a nor'easter blanketing Hartford with downed power lines, outages are simply part of life in Connecticut. Eversource and United Illuminating crews work hard to restore service, but what many homeowners don't realize is that the real danger often comes after the power returns—and that's exactly when appliance repair calls spike across the state.

This guide walks you through how to protect your valuable appliances before, during, and after a Connecticut power outage—because the last thing you need after weathering a storm is a dead refrigerator or a fried washing machine.

Why Connecticut Storms Are So Hard on Home Appliances

Connecticut averages one to three significant outage events per year. Major storms like Tropical Storm Isaias in 2020 left hundreds of thousands without power for days, and the nor'easters that sweep through from fall into spring regularly bring down trees and power lines across the state. Each restoration event carries real risk—not just from the outage itself, but from the voltage instability that follows.

Modern appliances rely on sophisticated electronic control boards that make them more capable than ever—but also more fragile in the face of electrical disruption. When Connecticut homeowners call for appliance repair in the days following a major storm, surge-related damage to those control boards is one of the most common culprits. Understanding why that happens is the first step toward preventing it.

Which Appliances Are Most Vulnerable During a Power Outage?

Not all appliances face the same level of risk. Those most likely to need appliance repair after a Connecticut power event are ones that combine a compressor or motor with sensitive electronics.

High-Risk Appliances to Watch After a Storm

  • Refrigerators and freezers — Compressors are especially sensitive to voltage spikes at startup after an outage.
  • Washers and dryers — Modern units with digital control boards can be rendered inoperable by a single surge event.
  • Dishwashers — Electronic control panels are vulnerable, and a mid-cycle outage can leave the appliance stuck in a fault state.
  • Ovens and ranges — Smart ovens and gas ranges with electronic ignition or digital displays are just as exposed as fully electric models.
  • Air conditioners and heat pumps — Compressor damage from surge events is a leading cause of HVAC-related service calls after storms.

If you've experienced multiple outages in a single storm season, cumulative surge exposure adds up—even if each individual event seems minor. Many Connecticut appliance repair calls aren't from one dramatic storm, but from a season's worth of smaller disruptions that gradually degrade sensitive components.

The Hidden Danger: Power Surges When Electricity Returns

Here's what most Connecticut homeowners don't realize: when power snaps back on after an outage, it doesn't always return smoothly. The initial surge of electricity flowing back through the grid can send voltage spikes racing through your home's wiring. These spikes might last only milliseconds, but that's enough time to fry sensitive components and turn a routine outage into an unexpected appliance repair situation.

The sophisticated circuit boards that make today's appliances "smart" are also exactly what makes them vulnerable. A voltage spike that older appliances would have shrugged off can permanently damage the control board of a modern refrigerator or washing machine—turning a five-minute power blip into a several-hundred-dollar repair bill.

Before the Storm: Quick Prep Steps for Every Major Appliance

When severe weather is heading toward Connecticut, a little preparation goes a long way:

  • Unplug sensitive appliances if an extended outage seems likely—including your microwave and any appliances with digital displays. Televisions, washers, dryers, and smart ovens should be unplugged, especially if they were in use when the power went out.
  • Turn your refrigerator and freezer to their coldest settings several hours before the storm hits. This buys extra time before food temperatures become unsafe.
  • Run your dishwasher and laundry cycles early. Getting caught mid-cycle when power drops can leave you with soggy clothes or a dishwasher stuck in a fault state.
  • Don't forget gas appliances. If your gas stove, dryer, or furnace has an electronic ignition or digital controls, they're just as vulnerable to surge damage as fully electric models.
  • Plug appliances into surge-protected power strips. Look for an on/off switch on the strip so you can quickly cut power if a surge occurs mid-storm.

During the Outage: Protect Your Food and Your Fridge

Once the power goes out, your refrigerator becomes a race against time. According to Connecticut Department of Public Health and FDA guidelines, a closed refrigerator will keep food safe for approximately four hours. A full freezer maintains safe temperatures for 24 to 48 hours; a half-full freezer, about 24 hours.

The key word is closed. Every time you open the door, you let cold air escape and warm air in. Resist the urge to peek. If you're unsure whether food is still safe after an extended outage, follow the rule: when in doubt, throw it out. Perishables that have risen above 40°F for more than two hours should be discarded.

Keep a refrigerator thermometer on hand—they're inexpensive and remove the guesswork from post-outage food safety decisions. A refrigerator that struggles to hold temperature after power returns can also signal a compressor issue caused by surge damage—one of the most common appliance repair scenarios we see in Connecticut following major storms.

After Power Returns: The 15-Minute Rule

When your lights finally flicker back on, your first instinct might be to plug everything back in immediately. Hold off. The grid can be unstable in the first several minutes after restoration, with additional surges possible as circuits come back online across your neighborhood.

Wait 10 to 15 minutes before plugging major appliances back in. This simple step lets the electrical grid stabilize and can prevent costly surge damage to your most valuable equipment.

Once you do reconnect your appliances, watch closely for these warning signs:

Warning Signs That May Require Appliance Repair

  • Error codes on digital displays. Modern refrigerators, washers, and ovens often show diagnostic codes after power events—don't ignore them.
  • Unusual sounds when compressors kick on. Grinding, repeated clicking, or a compressor that struggles to start can all point to surge damage.
  • Appliances that won't start at all. A control panel that stays dark or a motor that won't engage is a clear sign something was damaged during the outage.
  • Any burning smell. Unplug the appliance immediately and call for professional appliance repair in Connecticut right away.

When to Call for Appliance Repair vs. Reset It Yourself

Not every post-outage issue requires a service call. Try these simple steps before reaching out for help.

DIY Resets to Try First

  • Check and reset any tripped GFCI outlets (common in kitchens and laundry rooms)
  • Check your circuit breaker panel for tripped breakers
  • Unplug the appliance for 60 seconds, then plug it back in to reset the control board

When to Call a Professional

Some situations call for expert help. If your circuit breaker trips repeatedly, error codes persist after resets, the appliance shows no signs of life, or you notice a burning smell or visible damage, it's time to bring in a professional. At My Appliance Repair, we offer post-storm inspection services to diagnose surge damage and get your appliances running safely again. We've seen firsthand how Connecticut storms affect local homes, and we know exactly what to look for.

Don't wait for a small problem to become a major repair bill—contact our team or book a service call as soon as you notice something isn't right.

Surge Protection: A Smart Investment for Connecticut Homeowners

Given how frequently Connecticut experiences power outages, investing in surge protection is one of the smartest ways to avoid unexpected appliance repair costs. You have two main options:

Whole-Home Surge Protectors

Installed at your electrical panel, whole-home surge protectors cover every appliance and circuit in the house. They typically cost $200 to $500 plus installation by a licensed electrician, but they offer the most comprehensive protection available—especially worthwhile if your home has older wiring or has survived multiple Connecticut storm seasons.

Plug-In Surge Protectors

A more affordable option for individual appliances. Look for units rated for at least 1,000 joules for major appliances. These are especially worthwhile for refrigerators, washers and dryers with digital controls, and smart ovens or ranges. Make sure the strip has an on/off switch so you can cut power instantly during a surge event.

One important note: many homeowners assume their insurance will cover surge damage, but policies often require documentation that surge protection was in place. Check your policy and keep receipts for any devices you install.

It's also worth noting that Connecticut has a significant amount of older housing stock, and many homes still have outdated electrical panels that are more susceptible to surge issues. If your home was built before 1980 and hasn't had an electrical update, discuss this with a licensed electrician before storm season arrives.

Your Pre-Storm Appliance Checklist for Connecticut Homeowners

You don't have to wait for a downed power line to take action. Here's what you can do this week to get ahead of storm season:

  • Pick up plug-in surge protectors for your refrigerator, washer, and dryer
  • Get a quote from a licensed CT electrician for a whole-home surge protector
  • Place a refrigerator thermometer inside your fridge and freezer
  • Locate your circuit breaker panel and confirm all breakers are clearly labeled
  • Report any outage to your utility provider (Eversource or United Illuminating) so restoration crews can prioritize your area
  • If any appliance has been acting up since your last outage, schedule a professional appliance repair inspection before the next storm hits

Protect Your Appliances Before the Next Connecticut Storm

Connecticut's storm seasons aren't going anywhere. Whether it's the summer thunderstorms that roll through from June to August or the nor'easters that batter the coast from fall through spring, power outages will continue to be part of life here. But with the right preparation—and a smart response when power returns—you can protect your appliances from costly damage and avoid surprise repair bills.

If you've recently experienced a power outage and something doesn't seem right with your refrigerator, washer, dryer, or any other major appliance, don't wait for a small problem to become a big one. The team at My Appliance Repair is here to help Connecticut homeowners with post-storm inspections and appliance repair across the state. Visit us at myappliance.us, book a service call online, or contact our team to schedule service and keep your appliances running strong through whatever weather comes our way.
